errors.location: Proof of Theorem 1.1, construction of Y and extension of the automorphism of span{x_i}
errors.description: The separation of the translates of U does not ensure that span(Y) intersects L trivially. Therefore an automorphism of L cannot in general be extended while fixing every element of Y; the proposed construction can force the extension to be the identity.
errors.evidence: The proof asserts that each nonzero t in U is independent from {x_i}, then says to take any nontrivial automorphism of L and extend it by setting φ(y)=y for y in Y. For a counterexample satisfying all stated conditions, let G=Z₂⁶×K, K=Z₂^ℕ, with first-factor basis x₁,x₂,x₃,a,b,c and L=span{x₁,x₂,x₃}×{0}. Set U={0,a,b,c,a+b+x₁,a+c+x₂,b+c+x₃,a+b+c}×K. This is an open identity neighborhood whose L-translates partition G, so both conditions of Lemma 2.3 hold. Nevertheless x₁=a+b+(a+b+x₁), and similarly x₂ and x₃ belong to span(U); hence span(U)=G. Every maximal independent Y⊆U spans G, so fixing Y forces the identity on L as well.

errors.location: Theorem 3.1 and the unrestricted claims in the abstract
errors.description: The two-element discrete Polish group is uniquely homogeneous and has no nontrivial group automorphism, contradicting these statements. The restriction to more than two elements in Theorem 1.1 is necessary here too.
errors.evidence: Theorem 3.1 states: “A non-trivial Polish group cannot be uniquely homogeneous.” The abstract claims that every Polish group admits a nontrivial automorphism and that there are no uniquely homogeneous Polish groups. For G=Z₂ with the discrete topology, the only group automorphism is the identity. Its only homeomorphisms are the identity and the transposition, giving exactly one homeomorphism carrying any specified point p to any specified point q, precisely the manuscript’s definition of unique homogeneity.
